PI ENTERTAINS PSI UPSILON CONVENTION
Celebrates 75th Anniversary
ONE
of the most notable of the one
hundred and eight conventions in
the course of Psi Upsilon's 117-year
history was that held with the Pi Chap
ter at Syracuse, New York, on
Thursday,
Friday and Saturday, June 22, 23 and
24, 1950.
The time of the Convention coincided
with the 75th
Anniversary of the instal
lation of the Pi Chapter (June 8, 1875).
The celebration of the latter event
gave
an
especially festive air to the proceed
ings. Returning alumni recalled that the
Convention of 1925 was also held with
the Pi, on the occasion of its 50th An
niversary, and that the Chapter marked
its 25th birthday by entertaining the Con
vention of 1900. The Pi is akeady making
plans for its 100th in 1975.
The guests of honor at the 1950 Con
vention were the members of the Execu
tive Council, eleven of whom, including
all of the present officers and one
past
president, were in attendance. This is the
first time that the Executive Council has
been honored in this way. Estimates of
attendance vary, but it is safe to say that
not less than 300 members of the Fra
ternity were
present at one time or an
other, making this the largest Conven
tion since the Centennial in 1933. Over
250 attended the banquet on Friday
night.
In spite of the numbers, which ex
ceeded aU expectations, delegates and
guests were
comfortably housed and all
events proceeded smoothly and on sched
ule. This was, of course, due to able, longrange planning and efficient committee
work. Delegates enjoyed the benefits of
home life, being housed in the Pi Chapter
House, which overflowed with one of the
largest turnouts of undergraduate dele
gates of all time. The Fraternity is in
debted and wishes to express its apprecia
tion to Delta Kappa Epsilon, Phi Gamma
Delta and Phi Kappa Psi for extending the
full hospitality of their Houses to the Con
vention and thus adding greatly to the
comfort and pleasure of the delegates.
The Convention opened with registra
tion at the Chapter House on
Thursday
morning, and, after a buffet luncheon, the
first business session convened. Brother
Graham Margot, Pi '51, President of the
Pi Chapter, as
Acting Chairman of the
Convention Committee, expressed the
greetings of the Chapter to the Conven
tion, aiid introduced Brother LeRoy J.
Weed, Theta '01, President of the Execu
tive Council. Brother Weed thanked the
alumni and undergraduate Brothers of the
Pi Chapter for their hospitahty. Brother
Peter A. GaBauer, Pi '25, General Chair
man of the Convention Committee, took
the Chair as
Temporary President, and
appointed, by customary rotation. Com
mittees on Credentials and Permanent
Organization. After a recess to enable these
Committees to prepare their reports, the
Convention was called to order. Both Com
mittee reports were
presented and ac
cepted, and President Weed took the
Chair as Permanent President of the Con
vention. Members of the Executive Council
and other prominent alumni were intro
duced to the Convention, standing com
mittees were
appointed by customary ro
tation, and oral Chapter reports were
given
by a number of delegates (see page 113).
At the buffet supper at the Chapter
House on
Thursday evening, the under
graduates apparently got their first good
meal in several days. The caterer
reported
that the approximately one hundred and
fifty who were
present consumed the fol
lowing: 100 poimds of roast beef, 80
pounds of turkey, 50 pounds of ham, 20
pounds of tongue and 20 pounds of cheese,
with voluminous trimmings.
"Conventionality"
Having thus satisfied the inner man, all
settled down to
enjoy what the program
described as "The Perfect Performance�As
Good As It Ever Was or Will Be-the Ripe
and Mellow-Drama, 'Conventionality.'
"
This was a
repeat performance of the
103

skit presented by the Pi at the 1925 Con
vention, featuring several of the original
stars. It was a
lively representation of a
Psi Upsilon Convention! Petitions for Psi
U charters were
presented by Ezra
Whistlebritches, of Lydia Pinkham's Kowfrat, Hog Waller, Iowa; Labaleu Laval of
Canuck College, petitioning delegate from
the local "Axe Swingers" Society; and
Snow White, petitioning delegate from
"Nu Nu" and African Golf Society Insti
tute. The cast included Harry "Trusty"
Barber, Ron "Northwest" Putnam, Fraser
"Slim" McLennan, "Ringling Bailey" Barnum, George "Attic" Garrett, Graham
. "Oink" Davis, Eric "Candle" Will, and
Truman "Joe" Preston, all alumni of the
Pi Chapter. (Brother Will, who played a
petitioning delegate twenty-five years pre
viously, is the vice-president of Will and
Baumer Candle Company, and Brother
Preston is Judge of the Syracuse Traffic
Court. Incidentally, Syracuse has won the
Safety in Traffic Award for the past four
years, and the only "casualty" during the
Convention was a
parking ticket, all of
which bears testimony as to the efficiency
of Brother Preston's extra-Thespian activi
ties.) As Snow White, the latter brought
down the house, and won a charter for
his local society, by his rendition of his
classic composition, "Save a Little Dram
for Me." Jack Buckland acted as
manager
of the show.
Civic Luncheon
Reports from more of the Chapters were
heard at the Friday morning session, and
certain routine busniess was ttansacted. A
University luncheon for delegates, faculty,
city officials and visiting Brethren, at
Drumlins, followed, the guests being
transported by motor bus to this pleasant
spot with its country club atmosphere and
rural surroundings. More than 175 were
present, the overflow being seated in the
dining-room and cafeteria. The fact that
attendance was underestimated by almost
one hundred per cent occasioned a
delay
which allowed a chance for songs and
other delightful interludes, and gave the
older Brethren a wonderful time for remi
niscence and reunion.
Guests of Honor included Chancellor
William P. Tolley of Syracuse University,
Dr. Frank Piskor, Dean of Men, Professor
Lewis ("Doc") W. Crawford, Fraternity
Adviser, Mayor Thomas J. Corcoran of
Syracuse, George H. Bond, member of the
New York State Board of Regents, Trustee
of Syracuse University, and past national
President of Delta Kappa Epsilon, Brother
Weed, and Judge Truma'n Preston, who
regaled the luncheon gathering with anec
dotes about the Mayor of Syracuse and
repeated (by request) "Save a Little Dram
for Me."
Speaking on behalf of the University,
Chancellor Tolley said, in part:
"Apparently few people understand the
contribution made by fraternities to college
loyalty, to college scholarship or to college
ideals. The real significance of fraternities
is not the contribution they make to the
college housing problem, but their con
tribution to the development of the individ
ual. . . . Education is always the educa
tion of the individual. The fraternity never
forgets this. . . . The fraternity is concerned
with body, mind and spirit. Its goal is full
development of all potential gifts. This is
also the goal of the college.
"The public forgets that the goals of a
fraternity are identical with those of the
college or
university. They are
partners in
the same task. If the fraternity does its job
well, it makes no small contribution. . . .
"As the veterans graduate, we find our
selves once more in a world of pinkcheeked boys and wide-eyed dollies. Booze
and adolescence are like oil and water.
They simply do not mix. Fraternities
should set
higher standards of sobriety and
morality than the rest of the college popu
lation. Fraternities should raise the moral
tone of the campus and not lower it. If
they can
accomplish this they can
put the
rest of the college world on the defen
"Psi Upsilon has been at Syracuse Uni
versity for 75 years. It has made an incal
culable contribution to student and alumni
leadership. It has had high standards and
ideals. It has done much for its members
that probably could not have been done so
well by any other agency. There isn't the

Scholarship Awards
The Convention remained at Drumlins
for the afternoon business session, at which
the report of the Committee on Academic
Standing and Awards was
presented and
accepted. According to recommendations
contained in this report, it was announced
that the bowl, denoting the Chapter having
the highest academic standing, would be
given to the Iota for one
year, as well as a
plaque which will be the permanent pos
session of the Chapter. The plaque for the
greatest improvement during the period
from June, 1948, to June 1949, it was
announced, would go to the Eta Chapter.
(Formal presentation of the awards was
riiade at the Banquet on
Friday night.) The
report further recommended that an
ap
propriate plaque be awarded to the Delta
Delta Chapter in recognition of its out
standing record.
Annual Meeting of the Alumni Association
Following the adjournment of the bus
iness session, the Annual Meeting of the
Alumni Association of Psi Upsilon was
called to order by the President, Brother
Robert P. Hughes, Delta '20.
The following Brothers were elected to
the Board of Governors: Russell S. Callow,

106 THE DIAMOND OF PSI UPSILON
Theta Theta '16, Robert H. Craft, Tau '29,
J. J. Evans Hessey, Nu '13, Ray N.
Spooner, Lambda '15, G. Hunt Weber,
Eta '14, and George L. Brain, Iota '20.
The advisability of holding the Annual
Meeting at some time other than the after
noon of the second day of the Convention
was discussed, and it was the consensus of
opinion that the attendance would be bet
ter if another time were chosen.
Brother Hughes reviewed the activities
of the Alumni Association, including the
award of Psi Upsilon keys to outstanding
Juniors of the several Chapters, payment
for the cost of Phi Beta Kappa, Sigma Xi
and Tau Beta Pi keys won
by undergradu
ates, payment for the scholarship awards
made at the Convention, and financial as
sistance to the Executive Council in main
taining address lists. He pointed out that
there is an
ever-growing need for the
Alumni Association of the Fraternity as a
whole, as well as sound Chapter Alumni
Associations. The Alumni Association of
Psi Upsilon is ready, willing and able, he
said, to assist Chapter Alumni Associations
to
cope with their own
problems, but it
cannot and will not infringe in any way
upon the prerogatives of the Executive
Council, the Chapter Alumni Associations
or the Chapters themselves.
Convention Banquet
Albert C. Jacobs, Phi '21, Chancellor of
the University of Denver, presided as
Toastmaster over the Convention Banquet,
held at the Hotel Syracuse on
Friday night.
The Invocation, given by the Right Rever
end WiUiam P. Remington, Tau '00,
Suffragan Bishop of Pennsylvania, was fol
lowed by the singing of the National An
them and God Save the King. The Hon
orable Clifford H. Searl, Pi '05, Justice of
the Supreme Court of the State of New
York, who acted as Toastmaster at the 1925
Convention, delivered an address com
memorating the 75th Anniversary of the
Pi Chapter. With his great gift for oratory.
Brother Searl gave a beautiful kaleido
scopic review of memorable highlights of
the seventy-five years of the Pi, fifty of
which were so well known to him.
Brother Albert G. Hartigan, Pi '47,
author of "Brothers All," unfcjrtunately was
not able to be present for the dedication
of this new and already popular Psi U
song (see page 102). In his absence.
Brother Jack C. Buckland, Pi '36, led in
singing it.
Brother Jacobs introduced the follow
ing Brothers: Graham Margot, Pi '51,
President of the Pi Chapter; Edward C.
Peattie, Phi '06, Editor of the Diamond;
Dr. Charles F. S. Lincoln, Kappa '91, for a
quarter of a
century a medical missionary
in China, who returned to the United
States just twenty-five years ago in time to
attend the 1925 Convention, and who is
one of the most beloved of all Psi U's;
Robert P. Hughes, Delta '20, President of
the Alumni Association of Psi Upsilon,
who spoke briefly on
"Scholarship;" the
present and past members of the Executive
Council present: LeRoy J. Weed, Theta
'01, Allen Northey Jones, Beta Beta '17,
Benjamin T. Burton, Chi '21, Edward T.
Richards, Sigma '27, Robert I. Laggren,
Xi '13, John R. Burleigh, Zeta '14, Walter
S. Robinson, Lambda '19, Harold L.
Field, Upsilon '10, and Dan H. Brown,
Omega '16, all members of the present
Council, as is Brother Jacobs, himself;
and Earl D. Babst, Iota-Phi '93, who
served on the Council 1908-1928, and as
its President 1924-1928; Herbert Sherman
Houston, Omega '88, the oldest Psi U
present, who was saluted for his 66 years
in Psi Upsilon; Earle John Machold, Pi
'25; and Albert Blair Knapp, Pi '26.
It will readily be seen from the above
paragraph that the Executive Council was
well represented. However, the regrets of
many Brethren who could not attend were
perhaps, best expressed by Avery Hallock, Xi '16, in his absentee toast:
"To the 117th Convention of Psi Upsflon
To the 75th Anniversary of the Pi Chapter,
Greetings!
Our very best wishes especiafly to aU
brothers we know and in particular to
Earl D. Babst, Iota-Phi '93,
one of the greatest Psi U's ever, for his
tireless effort, his great 'Annals,' and
his undying spirit, magnificent
character, the inspirer of us all.
From the hetirt.
Biz and Abe Hallock, Xi '16."

Many communications
expressing re
grets and extending best wishes were
received from John V. Irwin, Delta '94,
Henry J. Fisher, Beta '96, John Godfrey
Saxe, Lambda '00, R. Bourke Corcoran,
Omega '15, George Henry Nettleton, Beta
'96, Reinald Werrenrath, Delta '05, Ken
neth A. O'Brien, Sigma '28, Stephen G.
Kent, Delta Delta '11, Frederick S. Fales,
Gamma '96, Francis N. Bangs, Lambda
'10, H. Percy Douglas, Chi '94, Herbert J.
Flagg, Theta Theta '12, Alfred H. Morton,
Omicron '19, Robert S. Taylor, Jr., Eta
'25, Robert G. Fufler, Mu '23, Henry N.
Woolman, Tau '96, Samuel L. Rosenberry,
Rho '23, Oliver B. MerriU, Gamma '25,
Edwin L. Garvin, Delta '97, J. J. E. Hes
sey, Nu '12, and many others.
Brother Jacobs directed the thoughts of
the assemblage to serious questions when
he pointed out that we are now
engaged
in a
great struggle testing whether our
way of life shall survive. "Never," he
stated, "has there been a
greater need for
men of intelligence, of courage, of wisdom,
than today. Never has it been more im
portant that public opinion be shaped by
sound judgment and by straight thinking.
The future of our
country, of the world,
and, yes, of civilization, is dependent on
the college men and women of today, the
leaders of tomorrow. This places a tre
mendous burden on our institutions of
higher learning, and fraternities are an
integral part thereof."
Brother Earl D. Babst, Iota-Phi '93, Past
President of the Executive Councfl, and
Brother LeRoy J. Weed, Theta '01, its
present President, spoke respectively on
The Executive Council Past and Present.
Brother Babst's address gave for the first
time a
comprehensive review of the activ
ities of the Executive Councfl. The Editor
feels that it should be printed in its en
tirety so that all members of the Fraternity
may come to know the tremendous scope
of the Council's functions and the res
ponsibilities undertaken by its members. It
will be found on
page 109.
By way of review of his service on the
Council, Brother Weed gave a
very stirring
address, and in particular he warned of in
roads being made by rather charlatan prac
tices on the part of certain organizers who
exploit youthful groups in various colleges
and universities. He referred to the great
contributions that had been made to the
Fraternity by various outstanding Brothers
who had served on the Council. He stated
that the activities of Council membership
were
purely labors of love and that the
Psi Upsilon Fraternity had never lacked for
men
willing to give their time and atten
tion to the Fraternity.
One of the high points of the evening
was the reading of a citation about Brother
Babst for his many and notablo services
to Psi Upsilon. He was presented with a
specially bound copy of the Annals of Psi
Upsilon, for the publication of which he
was
largely responsible, containing an en
grossed copy of the citation.
Final Business Session
At the business session on
Saturday
morning, reports of standing committees
were submitted and accepted. Suggestion
was made that the Chapters be given an
opportunity, some months in advance of
Convention, to suggest subjects for discus
sion at the Convention, and a resolution
was
adopted that such opportunity be
given and that a committee be appointed
each year to coordinate these subjects and
lay them before the Convention.
The Convention adjourned sine die at
the end of the session.
Clam Bake
Delegates and alumni adjourned, via bus
and car
pool, to the beautiful Skaneateles
Country Club, where something like a
mountain of clams was consumed and
where the celebration of the Pi's anniver
sary continued with unabated enthusiasm
during the entire afternoon and evening.
Although the country club had been hit
by a cloudburst, which left pools of water
all over the grounds. Dr. Lincoln had a
chance between occasional showers to pre
side over the annual undergraduate softball
game.
A real German band in costume made
for many hours of continuous singing.
While the weU organized clambake had
all the usual trappings, this anniversary

party was enjoyed the more in that it sup
plied an unhurried opportunity for many
of the alumni Brethren to re-live old times
with Brothers from Montteal to Florida
and across the continent.
(Editor's Note: The five delegates from
the Mu took advantage of the free time to
single out all the Pi Convention committee
chairmen to ask advice on the running of a
Convention, and even secured a
promise from
Executive Committee Chairman Charles R.
Ryan, Pi '21, and Finance Committee Chair
man, Donald B. Derby, Pi '18, to he present
at the 60th Anniversary of the Mu, where the
National Convention will be held next year.)
When the bake was served the club
house was filled to overflowing and the
guest book contained more than 250 signa
tures. The well filled Brethren sang for an
hour or more and could be heard for miles
around. After dinner they broke up into
groups and continued with revery and song
on into the night.
Highlights
The high tenor of the Convention was
sustained in large measure
by Pied Piper
Bishop Remington. His conviviality and
leading of all parades made for punctuality
at all functions. It can be stated without
reservation that he made a marked con
tribution to the success of the Convention.
Everyone was
thoroughly delighted with
the glorious Syracuse weather, except
when, at sine die, the "Chairman of
Weather" misjudged his assignment and a
cloudburst resulted in rather slippery foot
ing for certain Brothers as
they paid theiidevotion to Bacchus!
All will remember Brother Jack Zietlow,
Beta Beta '35, giving the Brethren the
benefit of his Yogi training when he "boxed
the compass," with the greatest of ease,
elevated his feet to the sky, and, while
standing on his head, gave thanks to Allah.
(Editor's Note: Brother Zietlow has indi
cated that he expects to submit to The Dia
mond from time to time contributions dealing
with the philosophy of fraternities. We look
forward to his efforts with great interest.)
The Upsilon had the largest visiting
delegation, thanks to Brother Field and the
always active interest of this sister Chap
ter.
For the first time, wire recordings were
made of the oral Chapter reports. These
recordings wfll be kept as
permanent
records in the Archives of the Fraternity.
To carry out the spirit of a resolution
which was
passed at this Convention, the
Pi Chapter dedicated a cabinet to hold
Fraternity pins of Brethren who wished
for a
place of safe-keeping. This cabinet
was
presented to the Pi Chapter through
the kindness of Donald B. Derby, Pi '18,
President of the Pi Trust Association dur
ing the Saturday morning business ses
sion, at which time the Convention paused
in silent prayer for deceased Brethren of
the Pi Chapter.
Honor Where Honor Is Due
Our Conventions, bringing men from aU
over the United States and Canada, in
volve tremendous expense, both in time
and money. They are
necessary in order
that the results of the past year may be
brought before the Fraternity, and an
op
portunity given to
plan for the future.
The Pi in 1925 saw the result of good
planning, and the success of the 1950
Convention was the reward of similar care
ful forethought. A committee was
organ
ized almost a
year in advance. Six months
prior to the Convention, the Pi's Executive
Committee decided to hold a
weekly meet
ing in order that problems might be dealt
with as
they arose.
Planning well in ad
vance did not place a burden on anyone,
and the confidence that was built up with
the passing months resulted in the well
attended, workmanlike meetings described
in the foregoing account.
The thanks of the Fraternity are due to
the members of the Pi who were
chiefly
responsible for the careful organization and
smooth running of one of the largest and
most successful of Psi Upsflon Conven
tions: General Chairman, Peter A.
GaBauer, '25; Co-Chairman, Joseph L.
Hueber, '24; Chairmen of Committees:
Executive, Charles R. Ryan, '21; Finance,
Donald B. Derby, '18; Banquet, Robert

THE EXECUTIVE COUNCIL
Address Delivered at the Convention Banquet
By Earl D. Babst, Iota-Phi '93, Past President of the Council
yOUR gracious words are
gratefully
received as a token to all members of
our Executive Council, past and present.
We are and always have been a team of
Brothers.
It is pleasing that this token is extended
at one of our annual conventions, and
especially on the 75th Anniversary of the
Pi Chapter, whose membership in all dec
ades has been such a source of pride to
Psi Upsilon. There are few greater honors
that can come to any of us, than mem
bership on our Executive Council. It is far
more than an honor. It is a rare
oppor
tunity to advance the noble design of our
fraternal bonds.
Notwithstanding its growth, Psi Upsilon
is still, as at its foundation, an
undergradu
ate institution. The return of alumni to the
chapter began immediately and through
the years has grown not only into a tradi
tion, but into active and organized sup
port. The early development, moreover, of
the Annual Convention and the establish
ment of its legislative functions gave sus
taining strength and vitality to the chap
ters. Later came the establishment of a
small co-ordinating body of alumni, under
the title of Executive Council.
So the primary elements which through
simplicity have contributed to the solidar
ity of Psi Upsilon are:�
undergraduate
supremacy, organized alumni support on a
chapter and national basis, annual conven
tions of chapter delegates with legislative
functions, and an Executive Council with
co-ordinating duties.
Aside from tasks specially delegated by
the Annual Conventions, the Executive
Council faithfully follows its traditional
role of acting as an auxiliary and advisory
body. It is not easy for an alumni group,
such as the Executive Councfl, always fac
ing a
procession of inquiries and problems,
coming from far and near, all to be re
solved on a
fraternity-wide basis, all form
ing precedents for future attitudes, to re
member that their executive function is
largely advisory. It is their success over the
years in this difficult role that has con
tributed to its high honor. With the
growth in the number of chapters and in
the membership, and with the policy of
avoiding professional administration, the
activities of the Council naturally expand
year by year. It is hardly to be expected
that the chapters, and the thousands of
living members, should even be aware of
the obligations of Council membership and
particularly of the responsibility resting on
the shoulders of its officers.
While humility and self-effacement long
have been characteristic of the Council's
services, yet on this occasion it may not
be amiss to glance at some of its activities.
It will be necessary to mention only a few
of the Council's routine duties, for all to
realize how far-reaching is its responsibil
ity�chapter visits, for example, which
bring the Council members into personal

Theta-(Vincent P. Donnelly, '51). The
Theta finds itself with a
depleted membership
following the graduation of eighteen Seniors

Academically, the chapter is above the frater
nity average and is doing well. In extra-curri
cular activities the chapter has men in every

sity teams. Members are active in the radio

President and Treasurer of the Junior Class.

a Finnish student and plans to support a Ger
man student during the coming year. The
chapter did well in intramural sports, finish
ing third out of nineteen groups. The social
year was a
great success. The chapter extends
a cordial welcome to all Brothers who come
to the Union campus.
DELTA-(Richard G. Myers, '51). During
the past year the chapter consisted of twentyfive men, of whom ten were Seniors graduating

initiated in September. The low chapter mem
bership has raised financial difficulties. Other

position. There is a

and one of the highlights was a week-end
party with the members of the Lambda chap
ter.

ma has had a low academic standing for the
past three or four years, but last winter the
chapter went up from seventeenth place to
twelfth place. Many expressions of approval

hopes that our
standing will be equally good

alumni membership, and the report was
very
favorably received and commented upon. The

blood donations to the local hospitals, assist
ance with Red Cross work, etc. Our most im
mediate problem revolves around the moving
into a new fraternity house as soon as the
University has made sufficient progress with
its new building program. However, we have
been fortunate in being able to obtain first
choice for a site in the new
"quadrangle," and
our alumni are active in raising funds for the
furnishing, equipping and endowing of the
new
property. Socially, the chapter has had an
excellent year, with several very good par
ties. It has been a
pleasure to entertain visiting
brothers from many of the New England
chapters and from the Eta chapter. The Sigma
extends its heartiest congratulations to the Pi
chapter on its 75th Anniversary, and further
congratulates the Pi chapter on its excellent
and comprehensive plans for the present Con
vention.
